extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, students of narratology, and general readers interested in story structure
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, describing, and applying Christopher Booker’s seven archetypal plot types and related narrative patterns (the meta-plot and rule of three) for analyzing or constructing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Meta-Plot (anticipation → dream → frustration → nightmare → resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meta-plot begins with the anticipation stage (the hero is called to the adventure), followed by the dream stage (adventure begins, early success, illusion of invincibility), then the frustration stage (first confrontation; illusion lost), the nightmare stage (climax where hope is apparently lost), and finally the resolution (hero overcomes burden against the odds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five stages as a high-level arc for a story centered on a hero’s development; they map beats from call-to-adventure through apparent defeat to ultimate resolution. Examples and stage labels are provided to help locate events within the arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-centric focus / character's self-realization
rubrics_metrics.description: "However many characters may appear in a story, its real concern is with just one: its hero. It is the one whose fate we identify with, as we see them gradually developing towards that state of self-realization which marks the end of the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories by the degree to which other characters and events illuminate aspects of the protagonist’s inner state and contribute to their progressive development toward self-realization; design characters as facets of the hero’s psychology rather than as fully independent centers if following Booker’s model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming the Monster
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist sets out to defeat an antagonistic force (often evil) that threatens the protagonist and/or protagonist's homeland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical structure centers on confrontation with an external antagonistic force; check for a clear monster/antagonist, stakes for hero/land, and a climactic defeat. Examples: Perseus, Beowulf, Dracula, The War of the Worlds, Star Wars: A New Hope, Jaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rags to Riches
rubrics_metrics.description: The poor protagonist acquires power, wealth, and/or a mate, loses it all and gains it back, growing as a person as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for an initial low status, acquisition and loss of gains, and moral/personal growth by story end. Examples: Cinderella, Aladdin, Jane Eyre, Great Expectations, The Ugly Duckling.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Quest
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist and companions set out to acquire an important object or to get to a location. They face temptations and other obstacles along the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence of an explicit goal/quest-object, episodic obstacles/temptations, a band of companions, and progress toward a culminating achievement. Examples: The Iliad, The Lord of the Rings, Raiders of the Lost Ark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage and Return
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist goes to a strange land and, after overcoming the threats it poses or learning important lessons unique to that location, returns with experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the contrasting ‘strange world’ episode versus ordinary world, the lessons/changes learned there, and a return that demonstrates gained experience. Examples: Odyssey, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, The Hobbit, Back to the Future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (pattern of confusion → single clarifying event → happy ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light and humorous character with a happy or cheerful ending; Booker stresses that comedy is more than humour — a pattern where the conflict becomes more and more confusing, but is at last made plain in a single clarifying event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge comedies by accumulation of confusion or misunderstandings that are resolved by a clarifying event producing a successful or happy conclusion. Many romance films fit this category. Examples: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Four Weddings and a Funeral, The Big Lebowski.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist is a hero with a major character flaw or great mistake which is ultimately their undoing. The protagonist's unfortunate end evokes pity at their folly and the fall of a fundamentally good character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence of a tragic flaw or error, a fall from greatness, and an emotional evocation of pity; tragic structure focuses on internal flaw leading to catastrophic outcome. Examples: Oedipus Rex, Macbeth, Hamlet, The Great Gatsby.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: An event forces the protagonist to change their ways and often become a better person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a catalytic event causing moral or psychological renewal and a demonstrable transformation by the end. Examples: A Christmas Carol, The Secret Garden, Groundhog Day, Iron Man.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Rule of Three (four forms: simple/cumulative, ascending, contrasting, final/dialectical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third event in a series becomes 'the final trigger for something important to happen.' Booker asserts the Rule of Three is expressed in four ways: the simple/cumulative three (e.g., Cinderella's three visits), the ascending three (each event more significant than the previous), the contrasting three (only the third has positive value, e.g., The Three Little Pigs), and the final/dialectical three (first two are wrong in opposite ways, the third is 'just right').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use threefold patterns to structure escalation, contrast, or resolution; recognize variants for pacing and revelation. Examples: Cinderella, The Three Little Pigs, Goldilocks porridge bowls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing works rigidly into archetypes (critique of Booker's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue Booker is too rigid in fitting works of art to the plot types and evaluates works on how closely they adhere to his archetypes; deviations are sometimes dismissed as flawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the seven plots as heuristic tools, not iron rules; be cautious about retrofitting complex or avant-garde works to these types. The page cites criticisms (e.g., Adam Mars-Jones, Michiko Kakutani) that caution against overextension of the scheme.
